# Accuracy at full data, and robustness {#sec-full-data}

With the full DrivAerML training split, in float32, GeoTransolver scores
0.0503, Transolver 0.0517 and ISLA's reference configuration 0.0552 on
surface pressure: ISLA is 10% behind GeoTransolver and 7% behind
Transolver. What separates the architectures is behaviour off the tuned
operating point. ISLA's reference frame degrades 1.2x under a 10:1
sampling-density bias where every configuration that centres on the
sampled points, GeoTransolver and Transolver included, degrades 10–16x;
under refinement its convention-swap penalty converges toward one while the
released baselines' stays at 3–7x. ISLA is covariant to rigid motions by
construction, and in arbitrary poses that exactness is worth 6% against a
rotation-augmented GeoTransolver and 19% against a rotation-augmented
Transolver. ISLA holds its accuracy across a decade of learning rate where
GeoTransolver degrades 4–14x on DrivAerML. Exact query independence, the
property that would make ISLA a true evaluate-anywhere surrogate, is an
optional configuration that costs 3.0–3.7x in accuracy; the reference
configuration does not have it. At 10,000 tokens on one GB300 the compiled
ISLA step is 47 ms in 1.30 GiB against GeoTransolver's 45 ms in 2.70 GiB
(@sec-cost). Across a flow-regime boundary, from attached to separated
flow or from low to high angle of attack, no architecture generalizes:
every one loses about a factor of ten (@sec-regime-extrapolation).

This chapter is the full-data counterpart of the small-data ladders in
@sec-data-efficiency, where GeoTransolver and Transolver are more accurate
than ISLA at every HiLiftAeroML training-set size measured. Here, at full
DrivAerML data, the ordering is the same and the margin is 7–10%; the
chapter's job is to state that margin precisely, what else is true of each
architecture at this operating point, and where all of them stop.

## In one paragraph {#sec-program-review}

At full DrivAerML data ISLA is 10% behind GeoTransolver and 7% behind
Transolver (@sec-full-data-accuracy); at 512 hidden width and 80,000 cells
per car the three are within 3% of one another. Where they differ is off
the tuned operating point: ISLA's reference frame is the one configuration
whose accuracy survives a sampling-density bias and converges under
refinement (@sec-robustness-density, @sec-consistency-bench), it is exactly
pose-covariant and leads the augmented baselines in arbitrary poses
(@sec-pose-contract), and it is robust to learning rate
(@sec-robustness-lr); its exact query independence is an optional
configuration bought with accuracy (@sec-query-independence). The
resources behind every comparison are in @sec-cost, the DrivAerML
measurements are collected beside their consistency columns in
@tbl-consistency-matrix, and the one axis on which nothing tested works,
extrapolation across a flow regime, closes the chapter
(@sec-regime-extrapolation). The book's single verdict is in
@sec-verdict; this chapter supports its accuracy and contracts clauses.

## In-distribution accuracy at full data {#sec-full-data-accuracy}

**At full DrivAerML data, in float32, GeoTransolver scores 0.0503,
Transolver 0.0517 and ISLA's reference configuration 0.0552: ISLA is 10%
behind GeoTransolver and 7% behind Transolver. On HiLiftAeroML the
full-split comparison is not yet measured.** The metric throughout is the
relative L2 error of surface pressure as defined in @sec-metrics: the
recipe's relative L2 on the standardized pressure field over the sampled
points of a case, cell-area-weighted, arithmetic mean over the validation
cases. The DrivAerML numbers are on the 48-car validation split of the
435-car training set (@sec-splits), seed means over two or three seeds,
evaluated in float32 at the final epoch of the frozen protocol of
@sec-protocol (10,000 sampled surface points per case, 500 epochs,
bfloat16 training, no augmentation, the freestream as a unit direction for
every architecture); no checkpoint was selected on validation error.
GeoTransolver is at learning rate 1e-3, Transolver at 3e-3 (0.0548 at 1e-3)
and ISLA at 1e-3. GeoTransolver's 3e-3 lane, which the protocol prefers for
it on this dataset (@sec-lr-protocol), is measured only in bfloat16, where
it is 3% better than its 1e-3 lane, so the 10% margin is a lower bound on
GeoTransolver's lead. The input scale is neutral on this dataset:
GeoTransolver fed the physical freestream velocity of 38.9 m/s scores
0.0498 against 0.0503 with the unit direction, inside the preregistered
null band (results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_drivaer_2026-09-09.json,
results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json; @sec-nb-fp32-drivaer-regrade,
@sec-nb-relframe-verdict).

The other ISLA configurations sit within 2% of the reference at this
operating point: the constant-gauge variant scores 0.0557, the
similarity-gauge variant 0.0543 at the same learning rate, and the
weights-off ablation 0.0542 (not adopted; @sec-mechanism). The
measure-weighted GeoTransolver and Transolver, research variants that
carry ISLA's quadrature measure in their slice pooling, score 0.0498 and
0.0522: the measure costs the baselines nothing here, and their lead over
ISLA is not a measure effect (results/mw_w4dr_xfam_reduction_2026-09-10.json;
@sec-nb-mw-verdict). The released GeoTransolver and Transolver are the
comparison; the measure-weighted rows locate a property and are not
modifications of those models (@sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines).

Those deficits belong to the reference size and resolution. At hidden width
512 and 80,000 sampled cells per car, in float32 and two seeds, the three
architectures are within 3% of each other: GeoTransolver 0.0419, ISLA's
constant-gauge variant 0.0428, Transolver 0.0431 and ISLA's
similarity-gauge variant 0.0431 (baseline ÷ constant-gauge ISLA 0.98 and
1.01 against 0.90 and 0.93 at the reference size), because ISLA gains most
from the cell count (16% from 10,000 to 80,000 cells against 8% for the
baselines) while width buys 9–11% for all three. The corner is stated with
its other coordinates. Density, in the sample frame a biased mesher
delivers: GeoTransolver degrades 10.5x under the 10:1 bias, Transolver
14.9x, the constant-gauge ISLA 16.6x and the similarity-gauge ISLA 1.09x,
so the similarity gauge is the only scaled configuration whose accuracy
survives a sampling-density bias, at the same cost as the constant-gauge
corner (22.9 against 22.8 GB, 0.281 against 0.285 s per step, 20.2 against
22.5 GPU-hours). Cost: the baselines reach the corner error at 0.3–0.6x
ISLA's GPU-hours (12.7 and 6.6 against 22.5) and ISLA holds it in the
least memory (22.8 GB against 41.5 and 27.6). What the corner demonstrates
is a frame class: a frame that does not read the sampling distribution
costs nothing at scale and removes the sensitivity. The similarity gauge
estimates its frame from the sample and pays for that on sparse
multi-element meshes (7.6% at 35 HiLift cases, 14.4% at the fixed angle;
@sec-data-efficiency); the reference configuration carries no sample
statistic at all, and it is not trained at this corner, so the corner has
no reference-configuration row (not yet measured). Down-transfer does not
improve with the gauge: queried at 10,000 cells the 80,000-cell
similarity-gauge model scores 0.0727, 1.69x its native error, against
1.55x for the constant gauge; deploy at the training count
(@sec-nb-scale-drivaer-synthesis).

On HiLiftAeroML the constant-gauge variant scores 0.041 at 1,260 training
cases (two seeds 0.040 / 0.043; results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json),
predicting drag to 1.4% and lift to 0.9% against the sampled-cell label
integral (results/hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json). No unit-drive
baseline and no reference-configuration ISLA is trained at that rung, so
the full-split HiLift comparison is not yet measured (@sec-program-status).
The largest rung with both is 510 cases, where GeoTransolver is 0.84x and
Transolver 0.90x of the constant-gauge variant (@sec-data-efficiency).

The comparison is fair by the criteria of @sec-fair-comparison: matched
tokens per case and epochs, each architecture at its own best learning
rate, shared validation cases, the same unit-direction drive, and a
matched parameter count (ISLA 8.9M against GeoTransolver 9.0M; Transolver
6.0M). Compute is close to matched at the reference size: at 10,000 tokens
the compiled ISLA step is 47 ms in 1.30 GiB against GeoTransolver's 45 ms
in 2.70 GiB (@sec-cost). The comparison is also narrow: two or three seeds,
one validation split per dataset, and no test-split evaluation of the
full-split models (the sealed test splits are spent on regime
extrapolation, @sec-regime-extrapolation).

## Learning-rate robustness {#sec-robustness-lr}

**Across the learning-rate grid ISLA's worst point is within 1.55x of its
best on DrivAerML and 1.14x on HiLiftAeroML, while GeoTransolver
degrades 4--14x at 1e-2 on DrivAerML.** The grid is {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2} on
DrivAerML and {1e-3, 3e-3} on HiLift, two seeds (42, 43) per cell except
the DrivAerML 3e-3 cell, which holds the three GeoTransolver seeds (42--44)
and five ISLA seeds (42--46) of the frozen-protocol training runs; every
other setting is held at the frozen protocol, and ISLA is the
constant-gauge variant. The quantity in @fig-lr-robustness is the
validation pressure rel-L2 defined above, evaluated in bfloat16 on
identical points (a within-grid comparison, for which the bfloat16
instrument is valid; @sec-metrics); a point is one seed and the line joins
seed means.

On DrivAerML, GeoTransolver at 1e-2 scores 0.739 and 0.221 on its two
seeds against its best of 0.0532, a degradation of 13.9x and 4.1x that
also differs by 3.3x between seeds. ISLA at 1e-2 scores 0.0874 and 0.0914
against its best of 0.0577, a degradation of 1.55x on the seed mean with
the two seeds within 5% of each other. On HiLift the same pattern appears
one step lower on the grid: GeoTransolver at 3e-3 destabilizes to 0.397
and 0.148 (9.4x and 3.5x its best of 0.042) where ISLA scores 0.045 and
0.049 (1.14x its best of 0.041 on the seed mean), and across the whole
HiLift grid ISLA's four results lie in 0.040--0.049 while GeoTransolver's
lie in 0.041--0.397. The robust architecture is the one whose worst grid
point is within a factor of two of its best; only ISLA satisfies that on
either dataset. The GeoTransolver lanes on both grids consumed the
physical freestream velocity. On DrivAerML that input is neutral (the
unit-drive GeoTransolver at 435 cars scores within 1.5% of the
physical-drive lane, @sec-full-data-accuracy), so the DrivAerML half is a
comparison between architectures. On HiLiftAeroML the physical velocity is
the input hazard of @sec-part-baseline, and whether GeoTransolver's
instability at 3e-3 there is a property of the architecture or of that
input is not measured; the HiLift half therefore reads as a measurement of
ISLA's own rate robustness (0.040--0.049 across its grid) and not as a
comparison.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lr-robustness
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Learning-rate robustness at full data. Validation pressure rel-L2
#|   (log scale, bfloat16 evaluation) against learning rate for GeoTransolver (red circles)
#|   and ISLA's constant-gauge variant (blue squares); small markers are individual
#|   seeds (42 and 43 in every cell except DrivAerML 3e-3, which holds
#|   GeoTransolver seeds 42--44 and ISLA seeds 42--46), lines join seed
#|   means. Left: DrivAerML, 435
#|   training cars, 48 validation cars. Right: HiLiftAeroML full split,
#|   1,260 training cases, the shared 180-case validation set. Protocol:
#|   10,000 sampled surface points per case, 500 epochs, bf16, no
#|   augmentation; the GeoTransolver lanes consumed the physical freestream
#|   velocity, which is neutral on DrivAerML and the input hazard of
#|   @sec-part-baseline on HiLiftAeroML, so the right panel's GeoTransolver
#|   series is not a comparison with ISLA. How to read it: the vertical
#|   spread of one colour across the grid is that architecture's
#|   sensitivity to learning rate. It does not show seed sensitivity at a
#|   fixed rate, which is a different property and is larger for ISLA
#|   (@sec-shared-floor), and it does not show any rate below 1e-3. Data:
#|   results/instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json (DrivAerML 1e-3,
#|   1e-2), results/mixedres_training_2026-07-31/sweep/round3_reduction.json,
#|   mt2_v3c_reduction.json and mega_reduction.json (DrivAerML 3e-3),
#|   results/highlift_wave_reduction.json (HiLift).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)
BLUE, RED = "#2a78d6", "#e34948"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})

RES = Path("..") / "results"
SW = RES / "mixedres_training_2026-07-31" / "sweep"
iw = json.load(open(RES / "instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json"))
round3 = json.load(open(SW / "round3_reduction.json"))
mt2_const = json.load(open(SW / "mt2_v3c_reduction.json"))  # ISLA, constant gauge, lr 3e-3
mega = json.load(open(SW / "mega_reduction.json"))
hl = json.load(open(RES / "highlift_wave_reduction.json"))

# DrivAerML grid: per-seed pressure rel-L2 at each learning rate
dr = {"gt": {}, "mt2": {}}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    for lr_key, lr in (("lr1e3", 1e-3), ("lr1e2", 1e-2)):
        dr[arch][lr] = [iw[f"iw_{arch}_{lr_key}_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
dr["gt"][3e-3] = [round3[f"gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["sweep_metrics"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
dr["mt2"][3e-3] = ([mt2_const[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["sweep"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
                   + [mega[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (45, 46)])
# HiLift full split: per-seed pressure rel-L2 at 1e-3 and 3e-3
hlg = {"gt": {}, "mt2": {}}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    hlg[arch][1e-3] = [hl[f"{arch}_hl_lr1_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
    hlg[arch][3e-3] = [hl[f"{arch}_hl_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]

style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver", "o"), "mt2": (BLUE, "ISLA", "s")}
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.0, 4.6), sharey=True)
for ax, grid, title in zip(
        axs, (dr, hlg),
        ("DrivAerML (435 train / 48 val cars)", "HiLiftAeroML full split (1,260 train / 180 val)")):
    for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
        c, name, mk = style[arch]
        lrs = sorted(grid[arch])
        means = [statistics.mean(grid[arch][lr]) for lr in lrs]
        ax.plot(lrs, means, color=c, lw=2.0, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3)
        for lr in lrs:
            ax.scatter([lr] * len(grid[arch][lr]), grid[arch][lr], color=c, s=16, alpha=0.9, zorder=4)
        # Direct labels at the midpoint of the last segment: GeoTransolver's steep
        # segment leaves room to its upper left, ISLA's flat segment to its lower side.
        xm = (lrs[-2] * lrs[-1]) ** 0.5
        ym = (means[-2] * means[-1]) ** 0.5
        txt = f"{name}\nworst/best = {max(means) / min(means):.2f}x"
        if arch == "gt":
            ax.annotate(txt, (xm, ym), xytext=(-10, 6), textcoords="offset points", color=c,
                        fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", ha="right", va="bottom",
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
        elif ax is axs[0]:
            ax.annotate(txt, (xm, ym), xytext=(6, -10), textcoords="offset points", color=c,
                        fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", ha="left", va="top",
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
        else:
            ax.annotate(txt, (xm, ym), xytext=(0, -12), textcoords="offset points", color=c,
                        fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="top",
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xticks(sorted(grid["gt"]))
    ax.set_xticklabels([f"{lr:g}" for lr in sorted(grid["gt"])])
    ax.set_xlim(6e-4, 1.6e-2)
    ax.set_xlabel("Learning rate [–]", color=INK2)
    ax.set_title(title, color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=10.5, pad=8)
    ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
axs[0].set_yticks([0.03, 0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8])
axs[0].set_yticklabels(["0.03", "0.04", "0.06", "0.10", "0.20", "0.40", "0.80"])
axs[0].set_ylim(0.026, 1.0)
axs[0].set_ylabel("Validation pressure error, rel-L2 [–]  (log)", color=INK2)
fig.suptitle("Learning-rate robustness at full data (points: seeds; lines: seed means)",
             x=0.02, ha="left", color=INK, fontsize=11)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.94))
plt.show()
```

The consequence for practice is that ISLA can be trained at a
protocol-default learning rate on a new dataset without a sweep, while
GeoTransolver's best rate must be found per dataset (it differs between
the two datasets here) and a rate one step too high can cost a factor of
ten. The scope is two seeds per cell (three to five in the DrivAerML
3e-3 cell) and two datasets; the grid does not
extend below 1e-3, and nothing here says where either architecture's
instability begins on other datasets. Robustness to learning rate and
robustness to seed are different properties: ISLA has the larger
seed-to-seed prediction spread on both datasets (@sec-shared-floor).

## Sampling-density robustness {#sec-robustness-density}

**Under a 10:1 spatially biased sampling density ISLA's reference frame
degrades 1.2x; every configuration that centres its coordinates on the
sampled points, GeoTransolver, Transolver and ISLA's constant-gauge
variant among them, degrades 10--16x.** The probe evaluates a trained
DrivAerML model on the 48 validation cars with surface points drawn ten
times more densely in one region of the car than elsewhere, with exact
Horvitz--Thompson measure weights so that any weighted integral is
unbiased; the readout is the ratio of the pressure rel-L2 under the biased
sampling to the same model's rel-L2 under uniform sampling at 10,000
points, in float32. A ratio of 1.0 means the prediction depends only on
the surface and not on how it was sampled. Every ratio states its frame:
the *sample frame* centres each model's coordinates on the biased sample
itself, which is what a biased mesher delivers and what ISLA computes
inside the model; the *pool frame* centres them on the uniform reader pool
before the biased draw, which hands a model an unbiased centre it would
not have in deployment. The sample frame is the headline convention;
pool-frame values appear only where they are the ones on file.

The frame is the pair of reference quantities a model uses to make
positions dimensionless: the origin from which they are measured and the
length that scales them (@sec-mt2). ISLA's reference configuration has no
origin at all: translation invariance comes from point-to-anchor vectors,
and the length is the square root of the total surface measure, an
integral the biased draw estimates without bias. The constant-gauge
variant centres on the unweighted mean of the sampled points, which moves
by 0.94 RMS radii under the 10:1 bias, and every downstream invariant moves
with it; GeoTransolver and Transolver consume absolute coordinates centred
by the datapipe on the same plain mean. The similarity-gauge variant
centres on the Horvitz--Thompson centroid and scales by the
measure-weighted RMS radius, so a biased sample estimates the same frame
as a uniform one; it is a sample-statistic frame that happens to be
unbiased, and it pays for its variance on sparse multi-element meshes
(@sec-data-efficiency).

| configuration | uniform 10,000-cell pressure rel-L2 | biased ÷ uniform, sample frame |
|---|---:|---:|
| ISLA, reference configuration (relative frame, total-measure scale) | 0.0552 | 1.24x (1.20 / 1.27) |
| ISLA, similarity-gauge variant (learning rate 3e-3) | 0.0616 | 1.21x (1.20 / 1.22) |
| ISLA, constant-gauge variant | 0.0557 | 12.0x (12.4 / 11.6) |
| ISLA, weights-off ablation (not adopted) | 0.0542 | 19.2x (23.4 / 15.1) |
| GeoTransolver | 0.0503 | 12.1x (12.0 / 11.9 / 12.5) |
| Transolver | 0.0517 | 11.6x (10.2 / 13.0) |
| GeoTransolver, measure-weighted pooling (research variant) | 0.0498 | 14.4x (14.3 / 14.6) |
| Transolver, measure-weighted pooling (research variant) | 0.0522 | 15.6x (15.9 / 15.4) |
| GeoTransolver, measure-weighted pooling and Horvitz--Thompson-centred frame (research variant) | 0.0505 | 1.04x |
| Transolver, measure-weighted pooling and Horvitz--Thompson-centred frame (research variant) | 0.0528 | 1.03x |

: Sampling-density robustness on DrivAerML, float32, 48 validation cars,
10,000 cells. Columns: pressure rel-L2 under uniform sampling; the ratio
of the same checkpoint's error under 10:1 spatially biased inclusion with
exact Horvitz--Thompson measure weights to its uniform error, with the
input frame taken from the biased sample (per-seed values in parentheses;
1.0 means sampling-independent predictions). All models are trained on the
435-car split under the frozen protocol; ISLA rows at learning rate 1e-3
except where stated, GeoTransolver at 1e-3, Transolver at 3e-3. The
measure-weighted and Horvitz--Thompson-centred baselines are research
variants that locate where the sensitivity lives; the released
GeoTransolver and Transolver are the first two baseline rows
(@sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines). Data:
results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json and
results/relframe_reduction_2026-09-11.json (reference row);
`research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_e_evalonly/campaign_e_density_fp32_sampleframe_2026-09-10.json`
(similarity gauge, constant gauge, weights off, released baselines;
@sec-nb-mw-postcenter); results/mw_w4dr_xfam_reduction_2026-09-10.json
and @sec-nb-mw-postcenter (measure-weighted baselines);
results/mwaw_2026-09-11.json (Horvitz--Thompson-centred baselines;
@sec-nb-mwaw-verdict). {#tbl-density}

Three things follow from the table. First, the sensitivity is the frame,
not the aggregation: measure-weighted pooling leaves the baselines at
14--16x, and an unbiased centre alone brings them to 1.03--1.04x, below
ISLA's 1.2x; ISLA's constant-gauge variant, which shares the plain-mean
centre, collapses with them (@sec-nb-mw-postcenter, @sec-nb-mwaw-verdict).
Second, ISLA's residual 1.2x with an exact or absent frame is the variance
of its measure-weighted routing integral under a 10:1 sample, not a frame
effect: given the exact frame of the full geometry as global data the
constant-gauge construction reads 1.13x, so the frame estimate accounts for
about 0.07 of the 1.2x and the routing integral for the rest
(results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json; @sec-nb-frame-full-verdict).
Third, the weights-off ablation is the most sensitive configuration
measured (19.2x), which is the deployment face of the in-distribution gain
it shows in @sec-mechanism. The similarity gauge does nothing for
zero-shot transfer to a held-out vehicle family, which stays at
mean-predictor level with or without it (@sec-limits), so absolute
geometric size is not what limits cross-family transfer. The scope is one
probe geometry (one bias pattern at one ratio) on one dataset; the
consistency benchmark below varies the sampling law and the count.

## Consistency under refinement and across samplers {#sec-consistency-bench}

**No configuration gives the same field under a different sampling of the
same surface at 10,000 cells; ISLA's reference frame converges toward it
as the sample grows, and the released GeoTransolver and Transolver do
not.** The density-robustness probe above changes the sampling
distribution by a factor of ten at one count. The consistency benchmark
(preregistered in @sec-nb-bench-prereg, verdict in @sec-nb-bench-verdict)
asks the question the principle of @sec-principle actually poses: does a
model converge to a single field under refinement, and to the same field
under two samplings of the same surface? Every checkpoint was evaluated in float32,
under its own training snapshot, on the same validation surfaces sampled
three ways from a 320,000-cell pool at 2,500 to 40,000 cells: uniformly
over cells (the training convention, which inherits the mesher's
refinement), proportionally to cell area (the law a uniform point-cloud
generator over the surface would produce), and with the 10:1 front/back
bias; each draw carries exact Horvitz--Thompson weights, so a
measure-consistent model sees the same integral under all three.

```{python}
#| label: fig-consistency-curves
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Convergence toward consistency. Each panel plots an architecture's
#|   pressure rel-L2 divided by the same architecture's error under uniform
#|   sampling at 40,000 cells, against the number of sampled cells, for the
#|   three samplers (columns) and three validation sets (rows); a curve that
#|   approaches 1 converges to the uniform-sampling answer. Uniform sampling
#|   (left) converges for every arm. Under the area-proportional sampler
#|   (middle) only the two measure-weighted ISLA arms on DrivAerML fall
#|   toward 1 (constant-gauge variant 2.6x, similarity-gauge variant 3.5x
#|   from 2,500 to 40,000 cells); the released baselines and the weights-off
#|   ablation are flat. Under the 10:1 bias (right) only the similarity-gauge
#|   variant reaches the uniform answer (1.028 at 40,000 cells). The
#|   reference configuration, benchmarked from 10,000 cells, is in
#|   @tbl-consistency-40k. The area sampler's Horvitz-Thompson
#|   weights span 1,000-37,000 (the bias probe's span exactly 10), so at small
#|   counts the refined regions (mirrors, slat and flap gaps) are unsampled
#|   and its fixed-count values carry information loss as well as variance;
#|   only the trend with count is interpretable. Legend: hue and marker identify the architecture and configuration. Markers are seed means over
#|   two seeds (raw values in the artifact). Float32; each checkpoint under its
#|   training snapshot. Data:
#|   results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json.
#| code-fold: true

# arm key -> (label, color, marker, linestyle)
STYLE = {

 ("HiLift, 35 training cases (180 val)", {"isla_const": "lad_hl_mt2_super_scarce", "isla_off": "a35_hl_mt2_noweights",

]
```

The same convergence appears when the training law itself changes. A
measure-weighted ISLA trained on the area-proportional convention and
evaluated on the uniform-over-cells one pays 2.9x at 2,500 cells, 1.45x
at 10,000 and 1.05x at 40,000 (the reverse swap 2.7x to 1.21x;
@sec-nb-mix-refinement), while at 10,000 cells the baselines pay 3–7x
with no count to appeal to (@sec-nb-mix-verdict). This is the consistency
criterion of @sec-principle observed on a convention swap: the two
conventions are two quadratures of the same surface integral, and the
estimator that treats them as such gives the same answer in the fine-mesh
limit. Two seeds, float32, snapshot code; data:
`results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_mixarea_2026-09-11.json`.

Three readings, in order of weight. First, consistency in the fine-mesh
limit is a property of the measure-weighted estimator standing on a frame
that reads no sample statistic. ISLA's reference configuration has that
frame by construction and shows the property: on DrivAerML its
area-sampler and bias dependence fall from +41% and +19% at 10,000 cells to
+3.4% and +2.5% at 40,000, and on the 35-case HiLift rung it is within
1.3% under the area sampler and 0.9% under the bias at 40,000 cells; on the
fixed-angle rung it converges to +2.6% under the area sampler and +5.5%
under the bias, still short of the 3% bar there
(results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_rf_2026-09-11.json,
consistency_bench_rffa_2026-09-11.json; @sec-nb-relframe-hl-bench). The
constant-gauge variant's sampler dependence is entirely its plain-mean
centroid: replacing that centroid by its Horvitz–Thompson estimate gives
the same field under all three samplers on DrivAerML at 40,000 cells (+3%
/ +3%) and on the HiLift 35-case rung already at 10,000 cells (−2% / +4%),
where the constant-gauge variant itself reads the distribution by 150% or
more (@sec-nb-bench-mcenter); the measure-weighted baselines reach the
same consistency once their datapipe centre is that estimate
(@sec-nb-mwaw-verdict), and those baselines are research variants that
locate the property, since the released GeoTransolver and Transolver are
not modified (@sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines). Among the configurations
run from 2,500 cells, under the area sampler the two measure-weighted ISLA
arms on DrivAerML fall steadily toward the uniform answer while the
released baselines and the weights-off ablation stay flat, and under the
bias the similarity-gauge variant reaches +2.8% at 40,000 cells; the
ordering by sampling-distribution dependence on DrivAerML at 40,000 cells
is similarity gauge, constant gauge, Transolver, GeoTransolver, weights-off
ablation (+18%, +90%, +213%, +562%, +1176%). Second, no configuration is
consistent at the 10,000 cells of the book's accuracy numbers, and the
factor-of-ten density probe understates how far each stands from
consistency: a different mesher changes the local density by thousands, and
at that scale even the measure-weighted estimator's variance is large where
the geometry is fine, so the area-sampler values at fixed count mix
information loss with model dependence and only the trend is read. Third,
on the HiLiftAeroML wings, whose refinement spans more decades than the
cars', the centred configurations do not converge within 40,000 cells; the
fine-mesh limit lies beyond the benchmark's range for them, and their
HiLift rows report the distance, not a verdict. What remains of the
reference configuration's dependence is the variance of the routing
integral under extreme weights, a limit that a sample budget alone does not
remove (@sec-robustness-density).

## Pose: a contract, not an accuracy edge {#sec-pose-contract}

**ISLA is exactly covariant to rotations and translations. When
geometries arrive in arbitrary poses, that exactness is worth 6% against
GeoTransolver and 19% against Transolver trained with rotation
augmentation; when every case is in the dataset's native pose, or a
canonical frame can be computed, it is a contract and not an accuracy
edge.** The first readout is float32 validation pressure rel-L2 on
DrivAerML with every case in its own random SO(3) pose: ISLA's
constant-gauge variant, trained without augmentation, scores 0.0566
(1.01x its native-pose 0.0558); GeoTransolver trained with SO(3)
augmentation scores 0.0602 (1.20x its native-pose 0.0503) and Transolver
with augmentation 0.0676 (1.31x its 0.0517); GeoTransolver without
augmentation scores 0.0631, and ISLA with augmentation 0.0578. Baseline ÷
ISLA is therefore 1.06 and 1.19 in arbitrary poses, ISLA's one measured
accuracy lead over input-matched baselines, and it is conditional on the
setting
(`research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_b_pose/campaign_b_fp32_2026-09-10.json`;
@sec-nb-pose-bench-book). ISLA's covariance is exact by algebraic
construction, verified to roundoff in fp64 (@sec-mt2); on the bf16 path
the recipe runs, the residual is finite (1.2--1.3% on scalar outputs in a
CPU autocast probe) and its value on the trained GPU path is not measured
(@sec-mt2-contracts).

The second readout is the native-pose comparison. GeoTransolver trained in
the native frame degrades 26--32x under random poses across three seeds.
GeoTransolver trained with the canonicalization of @sec-pose (freestream
to +x, roll fixed from the geometry's principal axes) scores 0.0536/0.0535
in-pose and 0.0536/0.0534 on the random-pose orbit, against 0.0530/0.0533
for the native-frame model in its native pose (bfloat16, same points):
exactly pose-invariant, 1.01x behind. Where a canonical frame exists, the
contract can be had for 1%. What ISLA's construction still buys is
generality: it needs no known global direction to canonicalize against and no sign-resolvable
principal frame, both of which canonicalization requires and both of which
every vehicle case here supplies (0 of 48 validation cars has a degenerate
frame). Where those conditions fail, on a geometry with a degenerate
inertia tensor or in a setting without a global flow direction, the
canonicalized model has no frame to compute, the augmented model pays the
20--31% above, and the equivariant one is unaffected.

## Query independence and its price {#sec-query-independence}

**In its reference configuration ISLA's prediction at a surface point
depends weakly on which other points were sampled with it, about 7%
against 2% for GeoTransolver; the optional query-independent
configuration removes that dependence exactly, at a 3.0--3.7x cost in
accuracy.** Query independence means that the prediction at one surface
point does not depend on which other points are in the same forward
pass. In ISLA's reference configuration, the one behind every HiLift and
DrivAerML surface result in this book, the output heads read directly
from the interacting encoder tokens, so redrawing the companions of a
point changes its prediction; holding a shared prefix of 5,000 cells fixed
and redrawing the rest of the 10,000-point sample moves the predictions on
the prefix by about 7% for ISLA and 2% for GeoTransolver. The
query-independent configuration (@sec-mt2) replaces the readout with
passive read blocks that read the slice and boundary tokens and never
write to them, so a point evaluated alone gives the same answer, to fp64
roundoff, as in a batch of 10,000; it has 11.0M parameters against 8.9M.
Its price on DrivAerML pressure is 3.5--3.7x against the reference
configuration at the same learning rate (0.203--0.211 against 0.0577) and
3.0--3.3x against a 6,500-token reference run at matched memory
(0.209/0.221 against 0.0697/0.0671, for an anchor-conditioned variant in
which a fixed core of 2,560 interacting tokens carries all the
interaction). The consequence is a choice, not a defect: exact
evaluate-anywhere semantics at about three times the error, or
GeoTransolver-class accuracy with a few percent of sensitivity to how the
boundary was sampled; not both. The interior task shows the same trade
from the other direction, less cleanly: the passive decode is about 3x
behind GeoTransolver-volume on interior pressure in float32, and admitting
the queries as interacting tokens closes that and more, but the two ISLA
configurations differ in decoder depth and inputs as well as in
interaction, so the 3x is the cost of the complete passive configuration
rather than of query independence alone (@sec-interior). The interacting
interior decode carries the same dependence as the surface one: its
prediction at a point depends on the joint query set, count augmentation
reduces that dependence by about 40% at a 3.7% cost and does not remove
it, so the model is deployed at its training query count
(@sec-nb-qcount-verdict, @sec-nb-relint-verdict).

## Cost {#sec-cost}

**At 10,000 tokens per case on one GB300, both models compiled as the
recipe runs them, ISLA's training step is 47 ms in 1.30 GiB against
GeoTransolver's 45 ms in 2.70 GiB (1.05x the time, 0.48x the memory) with
the geometry recompute on, and 39 ms in 1.94 GiB without it (0.86x).** At
40,000 tokens the default compiled ISLA step is 119 ms against
GeoTransolver's 53 ms (2.2x); with the exact fused geometry kernel, an
opt-in (`geo_kernel="fused"`), it is 52 ms at 4.5 GiB against
GeoTransolver's 10.0 GiB. The measurement
(results/kernel_study_2026-09-13/pareto_gb300_full_bf16.json;
@sec-nb-kernel-study) runs both models at the recipe dimensions (ISLA
hidden 192, GeoTransolver hidden 256, 12 layers and 256 slices each) under
bf16 autocast at batch 1 with an AdamW step, and reads peak memory and step
time in one harness; every kernel option agrees with the reference forward
to 5.5 × 10⁻⁷ relative L2 in bf16 and 10⁻¹⁵ in fp64, so no accuracy
number depends on the kernel. ISLA is the smaller of the two because its
relational readback pools the relational invariants over slices before
projecting them, an exact identity since the routing weights sum to one,
and recomputes the per-slice geometry inside the backward pass
(@sec-mt2-cost). The step is memory-bound at every stage but the MLP: the
per-slice relational invariants carry 61% of the memory traffic (38 of 62
GB per step in eager mode), which is what the fused kernel removes, and
the reason the compiled default's advantage over GeoTransolver narrows as
the token count grows.

## The frontier in one table {#sec-review-frontier}

Two tables collect the DrivAerML measurements of this chapter.
@tbl-consistency-matrix is the float32 standing of every configuration at
the reference size, accuracy beside consistency, with the scale corner
beneath it. @tbl-frontier is the bfloat16 table that covers the rows the
float32 matrix does not: zero-shot transfer to a held-out vehicle family,
canonicalized and rotation-augmented GeoTransolver, and the two-family
training runs. Every row of @tbl-frontier is trained on the 435-car
DrivAerML split at learning rate 3e-3 (the frozen rate, common to all
rows; the float32 figures at each architecture's own rate are in
@sec-full-data-accuracy), 500 epochs, 10,000 tokens per case, and scored
on the 48 validation cars. Its columns are:

- **In-family (x GeoTransolver)**: validation pressure rel-L2 at 10,000
  uniformly sampled points, divided by the GeoTransolver reference row's
  value; 1.00 is GeoTransolver's accuracy, larger is worse.
- **Zero-shot (fastback)**: mean normalized pressure L2 on the DrivAer
  fastback family (@sec-shift-suv), which no row trained on: the
  single-family rows trained on DrivAerML alone, the two-family rows on
  DrivAerML plus the estate family. Scoring every row on the same
  held-out family is what makes the column comparable down its length.
  A value of 1.0 is the level of predicting the mean.
- **Density (10:1)**: the degradation ratio of @tbl-density, biased over
  uniform sampling.
- **Pose (random SO(3))**: the degradation ratio of @sec-pose-contract,
  random poses over native pose; 1.00 is exact invariance.
- **Peak memory at 10k tokens**: peak training memory at 10,000 tokens
  per case, both models compiled on one GB300 (@sec-cost).

The frontier is stated as a matrix, not a column: every accuracy number
below sits beside the same checkpoint's behaviour when the sampling, the
pose or the vehicle family changes (@sec-principle).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-consistency-matrix
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
M = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "accuracy_consistency_matrix_2026-09-10.json"))
def f(v, fmt):
    return "not measured" if v is None else fmt.format(v)
out = ("| configuration | in-family error | density 10:1 (x) | pose, random SO(3) (x) "
       "| zero-shot fastback | few-shot gain from pretraining |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n")
for key in ("geotransolver_unit", "geotransolver_unit_mw", "transolver_unit", "transolver_unit_mw",
            "isla_reference_constant_gauge", "isla_constant_gauge_mcenter", "isla_similarity_gauge_lr1e3",
            "isla_relative_frame_ref", "isla_relative_frame_meas", "isla_frame_full_center", "isla_frame_full_frame",
            "isla_similarity_gauge", "isla_weights_off_ablation"):
    r = M["rows"][key]
    pose = f(r["pose_factor"], "{:.2f}") + (" (augmented)" if r.get("pose_note") else "")
    out += (f"| {r['label']} | {r['in_family']:.4f} | {r['density_factor']:.1f} | {pose} "
            f"| {f(r['zero_shot_fastback'], '{:.2f}')} | {f(r['few_shot_gain'], '{:.0%}')} |\n")
sc = M["scale_corner"]["rows"]
out += "| *scale corner, 512 wide × 80,000 cells* | | | | | |\n"
for key in ("geotransolver_unit_512x80k", "isla_constant_gauge_512x80k", "isla_similarity_gauge_512x80k", "transolver_unit_512x80k"):
    r = sc[key]
    out += (f"| {r['label']} | {r['in_family']:.4f} | {r['density_factor']:.1f} | not measured "
            f"| not measured | {r['gpu_hours']:.1f} GPU-h |\n")
print(out)
print(": Accuracy beside consistency on DrivAerML at full data, float32, unit-drive "
      "inputs for every architecture. In-family: pressure rel-L2 on 48 validation cars "
      "at 10,000 cells. Density: error under 10:1 front/back biased sampling with exact "
      "measure weights over the same model's error under uniform sampling (campaign E). "
      "Pose: error with every case in an arbitrary SO(3) pose over the architecture's "
      "canonical-pose error; the baselines were trained with SO(3) augmentation, ISLA "
      "without (@sec-pose-contract). Zero-shot fastback: error on 99 SHIFT-SUV fastback cases "
      "never trained on (1.0 is the mean predictor). Few-shot gain: improvement over "
      "training from scratch after fine-tuning on 20 fastback cases at matched learning "
      "rate. A configuration that reads the sampling distribution shows it in the "
      "density column; the weights-off ablation is the extreme case and is not adopted. "
      "The scale-corner rows (width 512, 80,000 cells, evaluated at 80,000 cells) show the three "
      "architectures within 3% of one another in-family; only the similarity-gauge ISLA corner "
      "(0.0431, 1.09x under the bias at 80,000 cells) keeps its accuracy when the sampling changes "
      "(all corner factors are sample-frame values at 80,000 cells; the artifact also carries the "
      "baselines' pool-frame values, 4.2x and 4.6x, which hand them an unbiased centre): "
      "it demonstrates the frame class (a frame that does not read the sampling distribution costs nothing "
      "at scale and removes the sensitivity). The reference configuration is the relative frame with the "
      "total-measure scale; it is not trained at the corner, so the corner has no reference row. "
      "The last column is training cost in GPU-hours. "
      "Learning rates are stated per row: the similarity-gauge checkpoints at 3e-3 sit beside the "
      "rate-matched constant-gauge variant at 0.0620, and the 1e-3 pair is at parity with the 1e-3 constant-gauge variant. "
      "The measure-weighted rows are research variants that give GeoTransolver and Transolver the quadrature "
      "measure in their slice pooling: their accuracy is unchanged. Density factors for all four baseline rows are the "
      "like-for-like values with the input frame centred on the biased sample, as ISLA's are; with the "
      "pipeline's unbiased pool frame the same checkpoints read 9.5x / 3.9x (unweighted) and 1.02x "
      "(weighted), so the pooling repair does not touch the frame, which is what the bias breaks. "
      "The measure-centred ISLA row is a sample-statistic frame and a variant, not the reference. "
      "Data: results/accuracy_consistency_matrix_2026-09-10.json (provenance per cell "
      "inside). {#tbl-consistency-matrix}")
```

```{python}
#| label: frontier-table
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path

RES = Path("..") / "results"
SW = RES / "mixedres_training_2026-07-31" / "sweep"
mega = json.load(open(SW / "mega_reduction.json"))
round3 = json.load(open(SW / "round3_reduction.json"))
mt2_const = json.load(open(SW / "mt2_v3c_reduction.json"))  # ISLA, constant gauge, lr 3e-3
probe = json.load(open(SW / "probe_reduction.json"))
p3v3 = json.load(open(SW / "p3v3_reduction.json"))
s1 = json.load(open(RES / "s1_similarity_gauge_2026-09-03.json"))["runs"]
p1pp = json.load(open(RES / "p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json"))["results"]

def mean(vals):
    return sum(vals) / len(vals)

# GeoTransolver reference: in-family pressure rel-L2 and zero-shot fastback, seeds 42-44
gt10_seeds = {s: round3[f"gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["sweep_metrics"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)}
gt10 = mean(list(gt10_seeds.values()))
gt_zs = mean([round3[f"gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["smoke_fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
# pose: random-SO(3) pressure rel-L2 over native-pose rel-L2, per seed
gt_pose = [probe["p1_rot"][f"gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["mean"] / gt10_seeds[s] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
mt2_pose = (mt2_const["mt2_v3c_seed42"]["p1_rot"]["mean"]
            / mt2_const["mt2_v3c_seed42"]["sweep"]["10000"]["mean"])
rot_pose = mega["gt_rotaug_seed42"]["p1_rot"]["mean"] / mega["gt_rotaug_seed42"]["in10k"]["mean"]
# density: biased over uniform (GeoTransolver seed 42 on the same instrument as the ISLA rows)
gt_dens = p3v3["gt_fixed_seed42"]["mean"] / gt10_seeds[42]
mt2_dens_const = [s1[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["p3_ratio_vs_infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
mt2_dens_gauge = [s1[f"iw_mt2_gauge_seed{s}"]["p3_ratio_vs_infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]

rot_in = mean([mega[f"gt_rotaug_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43)])
rot_zs = mean([mega[f"gt_rotaug_seed{s}"]["fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43)])
canon_in = mean([p1pp[f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["inpose_raw"][0] for s in (42, 43)])

mt2c_in = mean([mt2_const[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["sweep"]["10000"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)]
               + [mega[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (45, 46)])
mt2c_zs = mean([mt2_const[f"mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["smoke_fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
gauge_in = mean([s1[f"iw_mt2_gauge_seed{s}"]["infamily"]["pressure_l2"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43)])
gauge_zs = mean([s1[f"iw_mt2_gauge_seed{s}"]["fastback"]["pressure_l2"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43)])

mt2m_in = mean([mega[f"mt2_multi_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
mt2m_zs = mean([mega[f"mt2_multi_seed{s}"]["fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
gtm_in = mean([mega[f"gt_multi_seed{s}"]["in10k"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])
gtm_zs = mean([mega[f"gt_multi_seed{s}"]["fastback"]["mean"] for s in (42, 43, 44)])

GT_MEM, MT2_MEM = "2.70 GiB", "1.30 GiB"
rows = [
    ("GeoTransolver (9.0M), native frame", 1.0, gt_zs, f"{gt_dens:.1f}x",
     f"{min(gt_pose):.0f}--{max(gt_pose):.0f}x", GT_MEM),
    ("GeoTransolver + rotation augmentation", rot_in / gt10, rot_zs, "not measured",
     f"{rot_pose:.2f}", GT_MEM),
    ("GeoTransolver, canonical frame", canon_in / gt10, None, "not measured",
     "1.00 (canonicalized)", GT_MEM),
    ("ISLA (8.9M), constant-gauge variant", mt2c_in / gt10, mt2c_zs,
     f"{min(mt2_dens_const):.1f}--{max(mt2_dens_const):.1f}x", f"{mt2_pose:.2f} (exact)", MT2_MEM),
    ("ISLA (8.9M), similarity-gauge variant", gauge_in / gt10, gauge_zs,
     f"{mean(mt2_dens_gauge):.2f}x", "1.00 (exact)", MT2_MEM),
    ("GeoTransolver, two families", gtm_in / gt10, gtm_zs, "not measured", "not measured", GT_MEM),
    ("ISLA, two families, constant-gauge variant", mt2m_in / gt10, mt2m_zs, "not measured", "1.00 (exact)", MT2_MEM),
]
out = ("| configuration | in-family (x GeoTransolver) | zero-shot (fastback) | density (10:1) "
       "| pose (random SO(3)) | peak memory at 10k tokens |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n")
for (n, i, z, d, r_, m) in rows:
    zs = f"{z:.2f}" if z is not None else "not measured"
    out += f"| {n} | {i:.2f}x | {zs} | {d} | {r_} | {m} |\n"
print(out)
print(f": The DrivAerML frontier at full data, bfloat16 evaluation (ISLA rows are the "
      f"constant-gauge and similarity-gauge variants; the reference configuration's float32 "
      f"standing is in @tbl-consistency-matrix). In-family: validation pressure "
      f"rel-L2 at 10,000 uniformly sampled points on 48 cars, relative to the "
      f"GeoTransolver native-frame reference ({gt10:.4f}, seeds 42--44); all "
      f"rows at learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs, bf16. Zero-shot (fastback): "
      f"mean normalized pressure L2 on the SHIFT-SUV fastback family, which no "
      f"row trained on (single-family rows train on DrivAerML alone; "
      f"two-family rows on DrivAerML plus the estate family); 1.0 is the "
      f"level of predicting the mean. Density (10:1): pressure rel-L2 under "
      f"10:1 spatially biased sampling with exact measure weights, over the "
      f"same model's rel-L2 under uniform sampling (GeoTransolver seed 42; ISLA "
      f"seeds 42/43; pool-frame values for GeoTransolver, whose sample-frame "
      f"value is 12.1x, @tbl-density). Pose: pressure rel-L2 under random SO(3) poses over "
      f"native-pose rel-L2 (GeoTransolver seeds 42--44; augmentation and ISLA "
      f"seed 42; ISLA's covariance is exact by construction and verified in "
      f"fp64, so its ratio is 1.00 for every checkpoint). Peak memory at 10k "
      f"tokens: peak training memory at 10,000 tokens per case on one GB300, "
      f"both models compiled, bf16 autocast, batch 1, geometry recompute on "
      f"for ISLA (@sec-cost). Seeds per cell: GeoTransolver "
      f"reference 3, augmentation 2, canonical frame 2, ISLA constant gauge 5 "
      f"in-family and 3 zero-shot, ISLA similarity gauge 2, two-family rows 3. "
      f"Data: "
      f"results/mixedres_training_2026-07-31/sweep/{{mega,round3,mt2_v3c,probe,p3v3}}_reduction.json, "
      f"results/s1_similarity_gauge_2026-09-03.json, "
      f"results/p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json. {{#tbl-frontier}}")
```

The measure-weighted rows of @tbl-consistency-matrix are the steel-man the
principle asked for, and they split the story in two. Accuracy: once
GeoTransolver and Transolver carry the surface measure in their slice
pooling (@sec-nb-mw-prereg, @sec-nb-mw-verdict) they keep their
in-distribution lead over ISLA on both datasets, free on the cars and at a
6.5% price on the wings, so ISLA's contracts do not buy accuracy at the
reference size. Consistency: the pooling repair does not touch the frame.
Both baselines consume absolute centred coordinates, and with the centre
taken from the biased sample, as a biased mesher delivers it and as ISLA's
centred variants compute it in the model, the weighted baselines degrade
14–16x and the unweighted 12x (@sec-nb-mw-postcenter); the 9.5x and 3.9x
in the artifact are pool-frame values, measured with an unbiased frame
handed to them by the pipeline. Under a like-for-like frame only ISLA's
frames that read no biased statistic survive (1.2x), and the frame is the
whole of the density story at 10,000 cells for every architecture, which
is what the reference configuration's relative frame removes. The
measure-weighted and Horvitz–Thompson-centred baselines are research
variants that locate that property; the released GeoTransolver and
Transolver are the models compared, and they are not modified
(@sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines). What ISLA retains beyond
consistency is exact equivariance under arbitrary poses
(@sec-pose-contract), the interior velocity lead at matched parameters
(@sec-interior), and its memory footprint at scale.

Three things to read off the bfloat16 table below. First, at the common
learning rate the constant-gauge ISLA is about 1.2x behind GeoTransolver
in-family in bfloat16; the float32 figures at each architecture's own rate
put the reference configuration 10% behind (@sec-full-data-accuracy), and
the table's column is the conservative one for ISLA. Second, on the common
held-out fastback family no single-family row transfers: GeoTransolver
scores 0.59 (0.82 with rotation augmentation) and ISLA 0.95--0.99 in
either gauge, against 1.0 for predicting the mean; in float32 on two
seeds the unit-drive GeoTransolver scores 0.61 and the constant-gauge ISLA
at learning rate 1e-3 0.79 (0.98 at 3e-3). GeoTransolver's failure is the
milder one, but neither is usable, neither gauge nor pose handling moves
ISLA's, and a second training family moves both architectures to
0.11--0.13. Cross-family transfer is governed by training-data diversity,
with an architecture-dependent offset that does not change the verdict
(@sec-limits). Third, the two robustness columns are where the rows differ
by more than a seed spread: ISLA with the similarity gauge is the only row
of this table that is both sampling-robust and pose-robust without a frame
estimate, and the reference configuration, which is not in this table, has
the same two properties with no sample statistic at all
(@sec-robustness-density). At full DrivAerML data the gauge pays nothing
for this in the in-family column (0.0638/0.0629 against 0.0636/0.0627 for
the constant-gauge variant at the same rate), but at 35 HiLift cases it
costs 8% (@sec-mechanism); the memory column is the same for every ISLA
row.

## What is shared and what is not at full data {#sec-shared-floor}

**At full data, 70% of each architecture's residual is shared with the
other on identical points, seed disagreement does not predict error at full data,
and accuracy is still rising with tokens per case; the current
understanding is that both architectures approach a common floor set by
the protocol at this token count.** The measurements behind that
sentence are three.

The shared residual. Two GeoTransolver and two ISLA full-split
checkpoints (the learning-rate 3e-3 pairs on DrivAerML, the 1e-3 pairs
on HiLift) were evaluated on bit-identical validation points (10,000 per
case) and their four pressure residual fields were averaged point by
point; the shared fraction of a case is the measure-weighted energy of
that mean residual divided by the mean of the four models' residual
energies, so it is 1.0 when the four residuals coincide and 0.25 when
they are mutually orthogonal with equal norms. Averaged over cases it is
0.71 on DrivAerML (48 cars) and 0.70 on HiLift (180
cases).^[`results/n1_noise_floor_2026-09-01.json`, `shared_residual_fraction`.]
Whatever the two architectures get wrong at full data, they
mostly get wrong together, and equally so on the two datasets. This is
a measured fact about the residuals and nothing more; the probe cannot
separate shared inductive bias from any property of the labels, because
the four models share training set, pipeline, loss and point subsample.

Seed disagreement. On the HiLift full split, the per-case disagreement
between a model's two seeds correlates with its per-case error at
Spearman 0.15 for ISLA and 0.19 for GeoTransolver (this analysis scores
pressure on the gauge-pressure scale ‖p̂ − p‖/‖p − p_∞‖, a different
scale from the recipe metric, on which the same checkpoints read
0.11--0.12 rather than 0.041--0.042; the rank correlations are
scale-free), against about +0.6 for
both at 210 training cases and +0.67 for ISLA at 35
(@sec-data-efficiency). At full data, where a model is uncertain is no
longer where it is wrong, and two-seed ensembling gains only 3--4%. The
same artifact shows ISLA with the larger seed-to-seed prediction spread
on both datasets, which is why the learning-rate robustness of
@sec-robustness-lr must not be read as robustness to seed.

Tokens per case. Reducing ISLA from 10,000 to 6,500 tokens per case on
DrivAerML costs 8% in pressure error (0.0684 against 0.0633 at the same
learning rate), so at 10,000 tokens the error is still resolution-bound
rather than saturated; at 80,000 cells and 512 hidden width the three
architectures are within 3% of one another (@sec-full-data-accuracy). If
the shared residual is a floor, it is a floor of the protocol (the token
count, the sampled-point supervision, the labels) and not of either
architecture, and the flattening of ISLA's data-efficiency curve toward
1,260 cases (@sec-data-efficiency) would then be the floor asserting
itself rather than a property of ISLA.

The direct test is to train both architectures on the 1,260-case split
at 20,000 tokens per case and ask whether their errors move down
together, apart, or not at all. That is not measured
(@sec-program-status), so the statement stands as a current
understanding supported by three consistent measurements, not as a
result.

This is also the right place to state what the full-data result is and is
not. It is a two- or three-seed, one-split measurement that GeoTransolver
and Transolver are 7–10% more accurate than ISLA's reference
configuration at 435 DrivAerML cars in float32, and that the constant-gauge
ISLA reaches 0.041 at 1,260 HiLift cases with no unit-drive baseline
measured beside it. It does not say that the architectures are equivalent
up to that margin: on every HiLiftAeroML rung measured the baselines lead
by 12–32% against the reference configuration (@sec-data-efficiency), the
consistency and pose columns of @tbl-consistency-matrix separate the
architectures in ISLA's favour, and ISLA's passive decode trails by about
3x on the interior (@sec-interior), each in a different direction. Where
the protocol is perturbed the architectures come apart, and @sec-limits
collects where each one stops.

## Regime extrapolation: angle of attack and stall {#sec-regime-extrapolation}

**Trained on one flow regime, neither ISLA nor GeoTransolver predicts the
other.** Crossing from low to high angle of attack, or from attached to
separated flow, multiplies surface-pressure error by roughly ten for both
architectures, to a level worse than any architecture reaches from only
35 training cases inside the regime (ISLA's reference configuration
0.153, GeoTransolver 0.110, Transolver 0.114; @sec-data-efficiency). No
architectural choice tested here substitutes for training data that
covers the regime.

HiLiftAeroML (@sec-problem, @sec-splits) ships two curated partitions along
that axis. The **aoa split** trains on 788 cases at angles of attack of 12°
or less, validates on 112 further low-angle cases, and holds a sealed test
set of all 900 cases at 14° or more. The **stall split** partitions by flow
state rather than angle: 942 training and 135 validation cases labelled
pre-stall by the dataset, and a sealed test set of 723 post-stall cases. In
each split the validation set is in-regime, so the validation error
measures how well the model learned the regime it was shown and the test
error measures how far it carries beyond it. Training follows the frozen
protocol of @sec-protocol (10,000 sampled surface points per case, 500
epochs, bf16, no augmentation, learning rate 1e-3 for both architectures,
ISLA in its constant-gauge variant, seeds 42 and 43; 8.9M against 9.0M
parameters; memory and step time in @sec-cost). The GeoTransolver lanes
on these splits consumed the physical freestream velocity, the input
hazard of @sec-part-baseline, so the GeoTransolver rows are not a
comparison with ISLA; the finding of this section, a ten-fold loss for
every architecture, does not depend on that comparison. The sealed test was
run under a protocol declared before any test case was read: the eight
checkpoints were each evaluated exactly once on their own split's test list
with the frozen inference configuration, with no reruns and no
configuration changes after the numbers were seen.

The readout is the relative L2 error of surface pressure (@sec-metrics),
averaged over the cases of a split, and the degradation ratio

$$
d = \frac{\text{sealed-test pressure rel-L2 (other regime)}}
         {\text{validation pressure rel-L2 (training regime)}},
$$

computed per seed and reported as the seed mean, so d = 10 means the model
is ten times less accurate on the other side of the boundary than on
held-out cases from its own side.

| split | architecture | validation (in-regime) | sealed test (OOD) | d = test / val |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aoa | GeoTransolver | 0.0301 | 0.315 | 10.5 |
| aoa | ISLA | 0.0207 | 0.244 | 11.8 |
| stall | GeoTransolver | 0.0296 | 0.276 | 9.3 |
| stall | ISLA | 0.0207 | 0.260 | 12.5 |

: Regime extrapolation on HiLiftAeroML: seed-mean pressure rel-L2 on the
in-regime validation set and on the sealed test set of the other regime,
and their ratio d. Two seeds per cell; the per-seed values are the
individual lines of @fig-hilift-ood. Validation from
`results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json`; test and d from
`results/hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json`, whose `protocol` and
`inference_config` entries record the sealed-test declaration alongside
the numbers. {#tbl-hilift-ood}

```{python}
#| label: fig-hilift-ood
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Regime extrapolation on HiLiftAeroML under the one-shot sealed test.
#|   Left: the aoa split (788 training cases at 12° or less; 112 in-regime
#|   validation cases; 900 sealed test cases at 14° or more). Right: the
#|   stall split (942 pre-stall training cases; 135 in-regime validation
#|   cases; 723 sealed post-stall test cases). Each line is one seed, joining
#|   its in-regime validation pressure error to its sealed-test pressure
#|   error; filled markers are seed 42, open markers seed 43; red circles are
#|   GeoTransolver, blue squares ISLA. Each end is annotated with
#|   the seed-mean error and each line pair with the seed-mean d = test / val.
#|   What it does not show:
#|   per-case pairing or statistics (each point is a split mean over two
#|   seeds); anything about data efficiency (@fig-hilift-data-efficiency);
#|   velocity or wall-shear error. Protocol: 10,000 sampled surface points
#|   per case, 500 epochs, bf16, no augmentation, learning rate 1e-3 for both
#|   architectures, ISLA in its default constant-gauge configuration. Data:
#|   results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json (validation) and
#|   results/hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json (test, d).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)
BLUE, RED = "#2a78d6", "#e34948"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})

lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
sealed = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json"))
runs = sealed["runs"]
style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver", "o"), "mt2": (BLUE, "ISLA", "s")}
seeds = (42, 43)
# In-regime validation sizes come from the dataset's curated split manifests
# (112 low-angle cases for aoa, 135 pre-stall cases for stall); the sealed
# test sizes are read from the artifact.
n_val = {"aoa": 112, "stall": 135}
panels = [("aoa", "Angle-of-attack extrapolation\n(train at 12° or less, test at 14° or more)"),
          ("stall", "Stall extrapolation\n(train pre-stall, test post-stall)")]
X_VAL, X_TEST = 0.0, 1.0  # the only two x positions used; no per-series offsets

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.0, 4.9), sharey=True)
for ax, (axis, title) in zip(axs, panels):
    n_test = {runs[f"lad_hl_{a}_{axis}_seed{s}"]["n_test"] for a in style for s in seeds}
    assert len(n_test) == 1
    n_test = n_test.pop()
    for arch, (c, name, mk) in style.items():
        vals, tests, ds = [], [], []
        for s in seeds:
            key = f"lad_hl_{arch}_{axis}_seed{s}"
            v, t, d = lad[key]["pressure_l2"], runs[key]["pressure_l2"], runs[key]["d_axis"]
            assert abs(v - runs[key]["val_pressure_l2"]) < 1e-6  # the sealed-test file carries the same val number
            vals.append(v); tests.append(t); ds.append(d)
            face = c if s == 42 else "white"  # filled = seed 42, open = seed 43
            ax.plot([X_VAL, X_TEST], [v, t], color=c, lw=1.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=3)
            ax.plot([X_VAL, X_TEST], [v, t], ls="none", marker=mk, ms=7, mfc=face, mec=c, mew=1.6, zorder=4)
        vmean, tmean, dmean = (statistics.mean(x) for x in (vals, tests, ds))
        # Direct labels: seed-mean validation error left of the validation end,
        # seed-mean test error and d right of the test end. GeoTransolver sits
        # above ISLA at both ends, so its labels go above and ISLA's below.
        up = arch == "gt"
        ax.text(X_VAL - 0.06, vmean, f"{vmean:.3f}", color=c, fontsize=8.8, ha="right",
                va="bottom" if up else "top")
        ax.text(X_TEST + 0.10, tmean * (1.30 if up else 0.78),
                f"{name}\n{tmean:.3f} on test,  d = {dmean:.1f}", color=c, fontsize=9.0,
                fontweight="bold", ha="left", va="center", linespacing=1.3)
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xticks([X_VAL, X_TEST])
    ax.set_xticklabels([f"in-regime validation\n({n_val[axis]} cases)", f"sealed OOD test\n({n_test} cases)"])
    ax.set_xlim(-0.55, 2.35)
    ax.set_title(title, color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=10.5, pad=8)
    ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor"); ax.grid(False, axis="x")
axs[0].set_yticks([0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5])
axs[0].set_yticklabels(["0.02", "0.03", "0.05", "0.10", "0.20", "0.30", "0.50"])
axs[0].set_ylim(0.015, 0.6)
axs[0].set_ylabel("Surface pressure error, rel-L2 [–]  (log)", color=INK2)
fig.suptitle("Regime extrapolation on HiLiftAeroML: one-shot sealed test, one line per seed",
             x=0.02, ha="left", color=INK, fontsize=11)
fig.text(0.02, 0.02,
         "Filled markers: seed 42. Open markers: seed 43. Left end of each line: pressure error on held-out cases from the\n"
         "training regime. Right end: error on the sealed test split of the other regime, evaluated exactly once.\n"
         "d = test / validation, seed mean.",
         fontsize=7.6, color=MUTED, va="bottom", linespacing=1.35)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.09, right=0.99, bottom=0.27, top=0.80, wspace=0.08)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note title="How to read this figure"}
It says: *from either side of a regime boundary, both architectures lose
about a factor of ten.* The shallower red slope shows that GeoTransolver
loses a smaller multiple of a worse starting point. The vertical offset
between the colours is not a comparison between architectures (the
GeoTransolver lanes consumed the physical freestream velocity,
@sec-part-baseline). It does not show data efficiency, per-case
statistics, or any field other than pressure, and it is a two-seed,
one-shot measurement.
:::

Three readings follow, in order of importance. **Neither architecture
generalizes across a flow-regime boundary:** both lose a factor of about
ten, from 0.021–0.030 in regime to 0.24–0.33 on the sealed test, and those
test errors are worse than any architecture reaches from 35 in-regime
training cases (0.11–0.15; @sec-data-efficiency). A model that has seen
788 or 942 cases of the wrong regime is less useful than one that has seen
35 cases spanning both; coverage of the regime, not architecture, governs
this axis, and the other fields degrade the same way (sealed-test velocity
rel-L2 0.19–0.26 and wall shear 0.32–0.39 for all eight checkpoints,
against 0.04–0.06 and 0.07–0.10 in regime). **The absolute errors of the
two architectures on these splits are not a comparison.** The GeoTransolver
lanes consumed the physical freestream velocity (@sec-part-baseline), so
its in-regime 0.030 against ISLA's 0.021 and its sealed-test 0.315 and
0.276 against 0.244 and 0.260 carry that input; no unit-drive lane on the
regime splits is measured. **GeoTransolver has the smaller degradation
ratio because its in-regime floor is higher:** the two converge to similar
sealed-test error from different starting points, and a ratio criterion
rewards the worse starting point. The stall-split ratios are separated by
more than their seed spread (d_GT/d_ISLA 0.74 with disjoint seed
intervals), so the smaller ratio is a real feature of these numbers, and
the one mechanism proposed for it was tested and falsified
(@sec-ood-mechanism). The measurement is two seeds and one evaluation per
checkpoint with no per-case pairing; the ten-fold degradation is robust to
that. Both splits are drawn from one wing family; cross-family transfer is
treated in @sec-shared-floor and @tbl-frontier.

### The smaller ratio is not carried by raw coordinates {#sec-ood-mechanism}

**Giving ISLA a raw-coordinate input channel does not give it
GeoTransolver's smaller degradation ratio: the variant's d is 12.7 and 13.3
against ISLA's 12.5 and GeoTransolver's 9.3, and its sealed-test error is
unchanged (0.264 against 0.260).** The hypothesis was that GeoTransolver's
pointwise raw coordinates let it carry a learned map from position on the
wing to pressure across the boundary. The test adds those coordinates to
ISLA as a side channel appended to its seed invariants, deliberately
breaking rotation equivariance (a contract test asserts the break), with
the similarity gauge on; two seeds on the stall split under the otherwise
frozen protocol, and one permitted sealed-test evaluation of the two new
checkpoints only. Bars declared in readout units before training: raw
features carry the transfer if d ≤ 11.0 *and* sealed-test pressure error
< 0.245; they do not if d ≥ 12.0 *or* the error is ≥ 0.255.

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

res = Path("..") / "results"
b1 = json.load(open(res / "b1_raw_coordinate_discriminator_2026-09-07.json"))
lad = json.load(open(res / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
sealed = json.load(open(res / "hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json"))["runs"]

def ref(arch):
    keys = [f"lad_hl_{arch}_stall_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)]
    v = statistics.mean(lad[k]["pressure_l2"] for k in keys)
    t = statistics.mean(sealed[k]["pressure_l2"] for k in keys)
    d = statistics.mean(sealed[k]["d_axis"] for k in keys)
    return v, t, d

lines = ["| configuration (stall split) | in-regime validation | sealed post-stall test | d = test / val |",
         "|---|---:|---:|---:|"]
n_test = []
for s in (42, 43):
    r = b1[f"b1_hl_mt2_stall_rawcoord_seed{s}"]
    n_test.append(r["stall_test"]["n"])
    lines.append(f"| ISLA + raw-coordinate channel, seed {s} | {r['val']['pressure_l2']:.4f} "
                 f"| {r['stall_test']['pressure_l2']:.3f} | {r['d_axis']:.1f} |")
for arch, name in (("mt2", "ISLA reference (constant gauge), seed mean"), ("gt", "GeoTransolver, seed mean")):
    v, t, d = ref(arch)
    lines.append(f"| {name} | {v:.4f} | {t:.3f} | {d:.1f} |")
caption = (": Raw-coordinate variant of ISLA on the stall split against the reference rows of "
           "@tbl-hilift-ood: pressure rel-L2 on the 135 in-regime validation cases, on the sealed "
           "post-stall test, and their ratio d. Preregistered bars: raw coordinates carry the ratio "
           "if d ≤ 11.0 and test error < 0.245; they do not if d ≥ 12.0 or test error ≥ 0.255. "
           f"The variant's artifact records {n_test[0]} (seed 42) and {n_test[1]} (seed 43) evaluated "
           "test cases; the reference rows are means over the full 723-case test list. Data: "
           "results/b1_raw_coordinate_discriminator_2026-09-07.json (variant); "
           "results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json and "
           "results/hilift_sealed_test_2026-09-04.json (reference rows). {#tbl-hilift-rawcoord}")
display(Markdown("\n".join(lines) + "\n\n" + caption))
```

Both falsifier conditions fire on both seeds. The channel leaves in-regime
accuracy where the reference ISLA has it (0.0206/0.0201 against
0.0204/0.0210) and the sealed-test error where it was, so GeoTransolver's
smaller ratio is the arithmetic of a higher in-regime floor and not a
transfer mechanism its inputs carry; on the absolute readout there is no
transfer advantage to explain, and no GeoTransolver ablation removing its
raw coordinates is warranted.

**In practice, a regime boundary must be covered by training data; a
surrogate's in-regime accuracy does not predict its accuracy on the other
side.** A few dozen post-stall cases are worth more than hundreds of
additional attached-flow cases if post-stall predictions are needed, and a
validation set drawn from the training regime overstates the model's range
by an order of magnitude. Any reported accuracy for these surrogates
should state the angle-of-attack and flow-state coverage of the training
data alongside the error. Outside that coverage no architecture is
usable, and the choice between them is not the decision that matters.
